items.title: Home
items.text:
mibz2 decodes bzip2. It is block-parallel, as lbzip2 is. Within a block, its inverse BWT is walked as 32 interleaved chains, so a core keeps many of the walk's cache-missing loads in flight instead of one.

Think of a courier who learns each address only on arriving at the last one: the bike is fast, but most of the time goes on waiting to find out where to go next. That is the ordinary inverse BWT. mibz2 runs 32 such delivery chains through one dispatch centre, so while one waits for its next address, the others move. None of them travels faster; the waits overlap. Why 32 couriers beat one explains the idea, where it stops paying, and what has been measured.

  • Its output is byte for byte libbzip2's, and every block CRC and stream CRC is checked.
  • It runs on any x86-64 or aarch64 CPU. Its SIMD kernels (AVX2, PCLMULQDQ) are chosen at run time, and each has a portable scalar twin.
  • The library depends on std only.
>>> import mibz2
>>> data = mibz2.decompress(open("file.bz2", "rb").read())
>>> data[:18]
b'line one\nline two\n'
>>> with mibz2.open("file.bz2") as f:
...     lines = f.readlines()
...     verified = f.raw.verified
>>> len(lines), verified
(2000, True)

Its name is for "multi-chain inversion of bzip2". It was written in wikidata-pq, to decode the Wikidata dump, and knows nothing of Wikidata (history).

items.title: mibz2
items.text: A bzip2 decoder built for memory-level parallelism.

items.title: Where to go
items.text:
• Installation and the quickstart, in Python and in Rust.
  • What is checked, and when: each block's CRC before its bytes are returned, each stream's at its end, and what an error reports.
  • Why 32 couriers beat one: memory-level parallelism, the idea the decoder is built on.
  • How it works: the scanner, the workers and the multi-chain walk.
  • Benchmarks: master's figures over its commits, and mibz2 against the other bzip2 decoders.
  • Reference: the Python API, and the Rust API on docs.rs.

items.title: Install
items.text:
pip install mibz2   # Python 3.10+
cargo add mibz2     # Rust

items.title: History
items.text:
• In wikidata-pq. mibz2 was written in lmmx/wikidata-pq, whose split decodes the Wikidata JSON dump. A profile there found the bz2 decode about half of the split's CPU, bound by the inverse BWT's chain of dependent loads, and a prototype walked it as interleaved chains (lmmx/wikidata-pq#194). The production decoder followed behind a flag (WIKIDATA_BZ2_DECODER=native, lmmx/wikidata-pq#197): on CI, the split's CPU fell 20.6% and its wall 16.6% against lbzip2.
  • The bake-off. Before going further, it was timed against pbz2, fbz, the lbzip2 crate, indexed_bzip2, lbzip2 and libbzip2 on the dump's blocks. pbz2 0.2.0 tied it; the others were 1.5–1.9× slower at 4 threads (lmmx/wikidata-pq#199).
  • Its own repository. The decoder's history moved to lmmx/mibz2 by git filter-repo, its paths renamed and each #N in its commit messages rewritten to lmmx/wikidata-pq#N, with its journals. It was published as 0.1.0 and 0.1.1 on crates.io and PyPI, the crate and the Python package at one version.

The journals record each step.

items.title: Benchmarks
items.text:
mibz2's speed is measured on GitHub's runners by the Benchmark workflow (.github/workflows/bench.yml), with the A/B harness examples/ab.rs and bench/report.py. Nothing about performance is decided on a developer's machine.

  • History: master's figures over its commits.
  • Alternatives: the latest master commit against the other bzip2 decoders: pbz2, lbzip2, indexed_bzip2, fbz, the lbzip2 crate, libbzip2 and libbz2-rs.

These are decoder-level results: one process decoding one file, nothing else. End-to-end results, the decoder inside a pipeline, are in wikidata-pq's benchmark history.

items.title: What runs when
items.text:
event arms result a pull request that touches the decoder, the harness, the corpora or the bench its head and its base (the merge base with master), both built on the runner one comment on the pull request, edited in place on every push a push to master mibz2 and the alternatives the commit's result on the bench-results branch, and these pages the Actions tab either: a base commit given, as a pull request; none, as master the run's summary, not recorded

Pull requests never run the alternatives: their runs are the head against the base only. The alternatives that are Rust crates with dependencies of their own (fbz, the lbzip2 crate, libbz2-rs) are built into a second build of the harness, bench/alternatives, so the crate's own dev-dependencies stay as they are.

Only master's commits are recorded. A pull request's runs, and experiments that did not land, are not recorded or shown here; experiments are written up in the journals.

items.title: The workload
items.text:
• The crate's corpora (ab gen, tests/common/mod.rs), at scale 4, each compressed by libbzip2 1.0.8 at level 9: text (the crate's own sources and README, repeated: 12 MB), random (8 MB), onebyte (one byte repeated, 20 MB), pattern (a 7-byte pattern, 19.6 MB), runs (runs of random lengths, 10 MB) and records (binary records, 9.6 MB). The text corpus is made from the commit's own sources, so its bytes change a little from commit to commit.
  • The Wikidata dump's own blocks: 12 byte-range windows of 1 MiB of wikidata-20261019-all.json.bz2, at (2i + 1)/24 of the file. examples/windows.rs keeps each window's whole blocks, their bits untouched, as a stream of its own, checked against libbzip2 and lbzip2: 431 blocks, 11.85 MB of bz2 → 209.7 MB of JSON (17.69×). bench/wikidata.json pins each window's offset, length and SHA-256, and the corpus's. Wikimedia serves a dated dump for about six weeks, so the windows are kept on the repository's bench-data branch.

items.title: How it is measured
items.text:
• A run is one process decoding one file from disk, end to end, its output hashed (the same hash for every arm, or the run fails: the same-bytes check). It records the wall time, the CPU time (user + sys), the peak RSS, and each thread's CPU.
  • A round decodes every corpus once with each arm at each thread count: 1 thread (pinned to one CPU) and the runner's cores. The arms' order is rotated and reversed round to round. There are 10 rounds.
  • Block-parallel or single-threaded: each arm is classed in its records (parallel). A single-threaded decoder (libbzip2, libbz2-rs) runs at 1 thread only, once a round; at the runner's cores its figures are those 1-thread runs, paired with mibz2's at that count, and shown as 1-thread runs, never as a decode on more threads.
  • On a pull request, the base's own harness binary is an arm (mibz2@base/ab), so both builds run in the same process shape on the same runner.
  • Paired ratios: each round's ratio of one arm's time to the reference arm's (the base; or mibz2, against the alternatives), their geometric mean, and its 95% t-interval over the rounds. A change is called faster or slower only where the interval excludes no change.
  • The bench version (bench/report.py, semver) is stamped on every result. A change to what is measured or how is a new major version, and the history never joins a series across major versions, runner CPU models or sets of corpora.

items.title: The full-dump figure is modelled
items.text:
Each result also gives a whole dump's decode (103.5 GB of bz2), modelled, not measured, from the Wikidata blocks' runs, round by round:

  • the scanner's time (the one serial thread: each block's header and Huffman symbols) per byte of bz2, scaled by the dump's bz2 bytes;
  • the workers' time per byte of output, scaled by the dump's output, taken as its bz2 bytes times the sample's ratio (17.69×; another sample of the same dump, 24 windows of 25 MB, measured 18.68×; wikidata-pq's CI slice, lines recompressed, is 13.69×);
  • at N threads, the larger of the scanner's time and the workers' over N, times the sample's own wall over that bound; the same gap read as a fixed cost is given beside it.

It assumes time linear in bytes, the sample's mix standing for the dump's, and the runner's CPU; its interval carries the rounds' spread and the sample ratio's.

items.title: Modelled, not measured: a whole dump
items.text:
The decode of wikidata-20261019-all.json.bz2 (103 GB of bz2; 1.83 TB of JSON at the sample's 17.69×), scaled from the Wikidata blocks' runs above, round by round (mean ± its 95% interval, the sample ratio's own uncertainty added in):

mibz2 1 thread 56m33s ± 7m01s 4 threads 36m09s ± 5m11s 4 threads, the sample's overlap gap as a fixed cost 20m31s ± 3m19s the scanner alone (its serial part) 7m08s ± 54.7s the workers alone, over 4 20m31s ± 3m19s

At 4 threads the workers bound it. Per byte: the scanner 4.1 ns a byte of bz2, the workers 2.69 ns a byte of output at 4 threads (CPU, summed over them), 1.62 ns at 1 thread (wall, less the scanner's part); the scanner would bind from about 12 worker threads (mibz2).

What the model assumes - **Linear in bytes:** the scanner's time in the dump's bz2 bytes, the workers' in its output bytes. - **The sample stands for the dump:** 12 windows of 1 MiB at (2i + 1)/24 of the dump, 431 of its own blocks; their mix of entities and their ratio, 17.69× (the windows' 95% interval ±14.0%), stand for the whole dump's. Another sample of the same dump (wikidata-pq's bench/full, 24 windows of 25 MB) measured 18.68×; wikidata-pq's CI slice, lines recompressed, is 13.69×. - **The wall at N threads** is the larger of the scanner's time and the workers' time over N (the scanner is one thread; the workers run blocks in parallel), times the sample's own wall over that bound: its overlap and fill taken to grow with the work, which errs long. Read as a fixed cost instead, the same gap gives the third row. - **The machine is this runner,** reading the dump from page cache: no download, no disk, no other work. The output is hashed by the reading thread and discarded. - The uncertainty is the rounds' spread, with the sample ratio's added in quadrature to the part that scales with the output; not the runner's: another CPU model gives other figures. Loading the chart…

Master's mibz2 figures over its commits, oldest to newest. The chart above draws every figure at once; below it, one chart per corpus and thread count. Each point is a recorded commit (linked to it): the mean of its 10 rounds, and its 95% interval as a whisker. The figures are measured on GitHub's runners (methodology).

  • Separate lines, never joined: a line holds one runner CPU model and core count, one set of corpora, and one content of its corpus. Runners of one kind differ in speed from another (an AMD EPYC 7763 from a 9V45), so a commit measured on another kind of runner starts or joins that kind's line, in that kind's colour.
  • Joined only between neighbouring commits: where commits measured on other runners come between two of a kind's points, its line breaks, so no segment spans commits it didn't measure. Its points either side still compare (same runner model, same corpus); they are different runs on possibly different hosts, not a paired comparison.
  • Bench versions: a line runs on across bench versions that left these figures' meaning alone, and splits where a version redefined them (the benchmark's changelog). Each point's tooltip names the version that measured it.
  • text's points stand alone: that corpus is generated from mibz2's own sources, so its bytes change from commit to commit, and no two of its points are the same workload.
  • Trunk only: pull requests and experiments are not recorded.
  • Peak RSS is one of the figures (the selector above the charts).

These are decoder-level results. End-to-end results, the decoder in wikidata-pq's pipeline, are in wikidata-pq's tracker.

items.title: Concepts
items.text:
mibz2 decodes bzip2 as libbzip2 1.0.8 defines it, byte for byte, with every check libbzip2 makes, and decodes several blocks at once.

  • Why 32 couriers beat one: memory-level parallelism, the decoder's premise. One courier waits at every stop to learn the next address; 32 couriers' waits overlap. The lanes, the prefetch, the per-step cost that binds next, and the measurements.
  • What is checked, and when: block CRCs, stream CRCs, what an error reports, and the four inputs mibz2 refuses where libbzip2 does not.
  • How it works: the one sequential phase (the scanner), the workers, and the inverse BWT walked as 32 interleaved chains.
  • Prior work: libbzip2; Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi (DCC 2012); lbzip2 and pbzip2.

items.title: Block CRCs, before the block's bytes
items.text: Every block's CRC is checked before any of that block's bytes are returned. A block whose CRC does not match returns none of its bytes: the error comes instead. The bytes returned before an error are exactly the stream's up to the bad block.

items.title: Stream CRCs, at the stream's end
items.text:
Each stream's combined CRC is checked at the stream's end. The bytes of a stream's blocks are returned as each block is verified, before the stream's own CRC has been read. So a streaming caller has the whole stream verified only once a read reaches its end without an error: until then, what it has read is provisional.

In Python, BZ2Reader.verified turns true only when a read returns the end with every block's and stream's CRC matched.

items.title: Where an error was found
items.text:
An error says where decoding failed: in Rust Error { kind, block, bit }, in Python the DecodeError message. That is which block, and the bit it starts at. A damaged bit can be found later than where it lies, since the input is only known to be wrong once something it encodes fails a check.

The error kinds (ErrorKind):

  • the input: Empty, NotBz2, Truncated, TrailingData;
  • each of libbzip2's block checks: BadBlockMagic, BadOrigPtr, NoSymbols, BadGroups, BadSelectors, BadSelector, BadCodeLength, BadHuffmanCode, SelectorOverrun, RunTooLong, BlockTooLong, RunUnfinished;
  • BlockCrc and StreamCrc, with the stored and computed values;
  • this decoder's refusals: Randomised, BlockTooLarge;
  • Io (from a BzReader's source), RangeOvershoot, Cancelled, and Internal (a caught panic: a bug).

items.title: What is decoded, and what is refused
items.text:
The format is libbzip2 1.0.8's, with every check it makes: bzip2 1.0 and later output. Four choices differ from it, and each has its own error:

input libbzip2 mibz2 randomised blocks (written only by bzip2 0.9.0 and earlier, before 1999) decoded refused (Randomised) bytes after the last stream that do not begin another stream ignored an error (TrailingData): nothing after a stream is silently dropped an oversubscribed Huffman code pointing past the alphabet a stale table entry read an error a block whose compressed form passes 64 MiB (a real block is at most about 4.2 MB) decoded an error (BlockTooLarge)

items.title: Why 32 couriers beat one: understanding memory-level parallelism
items.text:
Most of a bzip2 decode is one loop, the inverse Burrows–Wheeler transform's walk, and that loop spends most of its time waiting for memory. mibz2 doesn't make memory any faster. It keeps many of the walk's memory requests in flight at once, so the waits overlap. That is memory-level parallelism (MLP), and it is the library's basic premise.

This page explains it with couriers and a dispatcher, then gives the mechanism behind each part of the picture, and the measurements so far. How it works has the threads around the walk, and Prior work the work it builds on.

items.title: One courier, one chain
items.text:
A motorcycle courier learns each delivery address only on arriving at the previous one: open the envelope, read the next address. The third destination can't be known before reaching the second. The bike is fast, but most of the time goes on waiting to find out where to go next.

That is the ordinary inverse BWT:

  • The table. After Huffman decoding and move-to-front, a block's last column becomes the T-vector: one 32-bit entry a row, holding the row's byte (bits 0–7) and the next row (the bits above). A block holds up to 900,000 bytes, so the table is up to 3.6 MB, larger than most cores' L2 cache.
  • The walk. Start at the block's primary index. Each step loads the current row's entry, writes its byte, and takes the next row from the same entry. The next row is anywhere in the table, so the load usually misses the cache.
  • The wait. The step after can't start until that load returns, because its address is in the load's result. A chain of dependent loads keeps one miss in flight, and the core idles through each one.
courier 1the corewaiting for the next address (a cache miss)idle: nothing to do until the address comes backa steptime → One courier. Each step (dark) is a few instructions; most of the time goes on waiting for the next address (light). Schematic, not to scale.

The walk was measured as latency-bound directly, on the machine where mibz2's prototype was built: walking 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 independent chains through one block, the cost fell from 28.5 to 4.4 cycles a byte of output (compute frontier, section 2). Memory bandwidth was nowhere near its limit. The walk was waiting, not moving data. libbzip2 and lbzip2 walk the one chain.

items.title: 32 couriers, 32 independent journeys
items.text:
Give each of 32 couriers a different delivery chain. While courier 1 waits for its next address, couriers 2, 3, 4… make progress. That is memory-level parallelism: the couriers don't travel faster, but there are enough independent journeys that waiting on one doesn't stop the rest. One courier is limited by the time it takes to get each new address; 32 keep many requests in flight.

courier 1courier 2courier 3courier 4the coreslots for couriers 5 to 32each courier's step, one after anothertime → Four of mibz2's 32 couriers. Each still waits as long for its address, but the waits overlap, and the core takes the other couriers' steps in the gaps. Schematic, not to scale.

The correction that keeps the picture faithful

The CPU doesn't employ 32 workers, and the lanes aren't threads. One core interleaves the instructions of 32 traversal chains, and its out-of-order machinery overlaps their memory requests. The better image is one dispatch centre managing 32 motorcycles, each getting its next destination only when its last delivery returns an address.

What counts is deliveries a second for the whole centre, not how fast one bike finishes its route: sustained throughput, not the latency of any one load. Every load still takes as long as before.

Several threads are several dispatch centres, one a block: mibz2's workers decode whole blocks in parallel (How it works). The lanes are the parallelism inside each one.

items.title: Where the independent journeys come from
items.text:
A block has one chain, not 32: the T-vector is a single cycle through every row (or, for a periodic text, a few). bzip2 carries no metadata to start a walk anywhere but the primary index. mibz2 makes the journeys itself:

  • Random starts. 511 pseudo-random rows, plus the walk's own first row, become segment starts. A random row is a random position in the text, so the cycle is cut into 512 segments of about equal length. (Evenly spaced rows clustered in the text and stalled the lanes.)
  • Flagged starts end a segment. Each start is flagged in bit 31 of its own T-vector entry, which links never use. A lane that reads a flagged entry has run into the next segment's start: its segment ends there, recording which start it ran into, and the lane takes the next unwalked segment.
  • 32 lanes walk in lockstep. Each round, every lane takes one step, writing its byte into its own segment's buffer.
  • The segments are stitched together afterwards. From the first row's segment, each segment is followed by the one it ran into, until the block's length is reached. The output is exactly the plain walk's, byte for byte, including a periodic block's several cycles. The flags are cleared before the walk returns.
  • Short blocks walk plainly. Under 64 KiB, the segments' bookkeeping costs more than the waits it hides; only a stream's last block is ever that short.
one chaincut at startsjoinedthe plain walk: one courier, row after row, from the primary index to the block's endA · lane 1B · lane 3C · lane 2D · lane 4E · lane 2F · lane 1G · lane 4H · lane 3▼ a start row, flagged in its own entry: the segment before it ends there, and a lane takes the nextA, then the segment A ran into (B), then C… until the block's length: exactly the plain walk's bytes One chain cut at flagged starts into segments, walked by four lanes in whatever order the lanes take them, then joined in order. mibz2 cuts each block into 512 segments for 32 lanes.

items.title: Prefetching: phoning ahead
items.text:
Lanes alone weren't enough. Without help, a lane's next load is issued only when its instructions enter the core's reorder buffer, which is full of the other lanes' steps. So the misses in flight were bounded by how many steps that window holds, and adding lanes didn't add misses.

mibz2 issues a software prefetch of each lane's next entry as soon as its row is known (prefetcht0 on x86-64, prfm pldl1keep on aarch64). A prefetch retires without waiting for its data, so every lane's miss starts at once. In the picture, the dispatcher phones each request through the moment an address is read, rather than when that courier's turn comes round on the board.

Try the counts yourself in this schematic. It has one dispatcher, whose paperwork for a step takes a tick or two, and each address takes 31 ticks to come back. The timings are made up for the picture.

The schematic needs JavaScript.

items.title: The dispatcher becomes the bottleneck
items.text:
There is only so much road, and one dispatcher. Add enough couriers and every wait is covered. Then the limit is the dispatcher: each step's paperwork, done for each courier in turn. Add more couriers past that point and the dispatcher spends more on coordination than the extra journeys earn.

In the core, the dispatcher's limits are these:

  • Instructions a step. Every lane's step is a handful of instructions: the load, the flag test, the byte's store, the write pointer's advance, the buffer-end check, the prefetch. With the misses overlapped, the walk runs at the rate the core can issue those instructions.
  • Register pressure. One lane's state (its row, its write pointers, its segment) fits in registers, but 32 lanes' state doesn't. It lives in the L1 cache, and every step loads and stores some of it.
  • Cache contention. The lanes' table lines, the 512 segments' buffers and the lanes' own state share the same caches. At four threads, four walks share the L3.
  • Outstanding misses. A core tracks only so many misses at once (its line fill buffers, and the L2's own queue). Beyond that, more lanes only queue.

The record shows both sides. Without the prefetch, 16 lanes were within noise of 12, and 24 or 32 were slower (PR #21). With it, 16 to 32 lanes were about 26–28% faster than 12 lanes without it, and within noise of each other at one walk. With four walks at once, 32 lanes won clearly. So mibz2 runs 32 lanes and 512 segments (the measured points).

It also explains why a cleverer-looking algorithm can lose. Once 32 misses are in flight, the walk is bound by instructions a step, not by the latency of each load. A change that saves steps but makes each one dearer loses. A change that keeps the steps and makes them cheaper wins.

items.title: Make the dispatcher efficient
items.text:
Once there are enough couriers, cut the paperwork a step. That's how the walk got faster:

  • The flagged walk (#12). It replaced the first segmented walk, which tested every step's row against a separate bitmap of the starts (12 lanes, 256 segments). The flag moved into the entry the step loads anyway, bytes went out through raw per-lane pointers instead of a growable vector's push, and the test for idle lanes left the hot loop.
  • The prefetch, with 32 lanes and 512 segments (#21): every lane's next miss starts at once, as above.
  • The shared-offset walk, after libsais's chain decode (#37, the default walk since 0.1.5). libsais 2.12's decode_chains runs room rounds of every chain at a shared output offset, where room is the fewest bytes any chain's buffer has spare. Within a pass, a lane's byte goes to its buffer's base plus the pass's offset, so the per-step pointer store and buffer-end test are gone. The lanes, the prefetch and the segments are unchanged, so the same misses are in flight. Only the instructions a step drop: one dispatcher's paperwork, done in batches.

Two cleverer-looking ideas from the literature were built, measured and dropped. Both changed the journeys themselves, and both lost to their extra cost a step:

  • The pair walk, ψ² (#34, after libsais and Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi's super-alphabet). Each entry holds the row two steps on, so the walk takes half the steps, two bytes at each. But each step costs about twice as much: the second byte comes from a first-byte lookup. With the prefetch keeping 32 misses in flight, halving the dependent loads bought almost nothing, and the pair table took about three times as long to build. Envelopes holding two addresses mean fewer stops, but twice the paperwork at each, and the envelopes take three times as long to fill.
  • Precopy (#36, after Kärkkäinen and Puglisi). Where a stretch of the walk repeats one already walked, its bytes are copied instead of walked. It copied 31.5% of the Wikidata blocks' bytes, and was slower all the same. The repeat check ran on every step, and the steps it skipped were the cheap ones, whose table lines were already in cache. The cost is in the scattered steps, which repeats never cover. A courier who checks the logbook for a repeated stretch at every stop loses more time than the short, nearby stretches it saves.
flagged walk (the default before #37): a step's journey, then its bookkeepingshared-offset walk (#37, the default): the same journeys, less bookkeeping a steppair walk, ψ² (#34, lost): two bytes a step, about twice the work a stepPrecopy (#36, lost): a repeat check on every step; the copies skip only cheap stepsthe journey: load the entry, take its bytebookkeeping: flags, pointers, buffer ends, checksa byte out The core's time once enough misses are in flight, schematically: the bytes out in the same time. The shared-offset walk keeps the journeys and cuts the bookkeeping. The pair walk halves the steps but doubles each one's work, and pays again in its build. Precopy adds a check to every step to skip a few cheap ones.

items.title: The measurements
items.text:
Read these as indicative

These are the walk alone, on one thread, mostly on shared development machines. Each comparison holds only within its own row: the rows differ in machine, clock, corpus and repeats. The implementations differ in more than their lane count, too: the bitmap or the flag, the vector push or the raw pointers, the prefetch, and the segment count. Only the CI benchmark decides what merges.

items.title: The whole decoder, on CI
items.text:
The walk is about 53–60% of a decode, so a walk change moves the whole decoder by less. Whole-decoder figures come only from the CI benchmark: paired rounds of a pull request's head against its base on one runner (methodology). The walk's changes, on the Wikidata blocks (wall time, head over base, with its 95% interval; − is faster):

change 1 thread 4 threads bench the flagged walk (#12) −10.7% (−11.3%, −10.2%) −16.6% (−18.2%, −15.0%) #12 32 lanes, 512 segments, the prefetch (#21) −13.2% (−13.8%, −12.5%) −8.3% (−11.5%, −5.0%) #21 the pair walk, ψ² (#34, not merged) +40.6% (+40.1%, +41.1%) +24.3% (+22.8%, +25.8%) #34 Precopy (#36, not merged) +18.0% (+15.9%, +20.1%) +6.0% (+5.0%, +6.9%) #36 the shared-offset walk (#37) −10.3% (−10.6%, −10.0%) −9.1% (−12.2%, −5.9%) #37, its first run (EPYC 9V74); its last, on a Xeon 6973P-C: −5.8% (−7.3%, −4.2%) and −2.7% (−4.1%, −1.3%)

Each row is its own runner and its own base, so the rows don't add up. Master's figures over its commits are on the History page, and mibz2 beside the other bzip2 decoders on Alternatives.

items.title: The picture, term by term
items.text: in the picture in the decoder a courier a lane: one traversal chain, walking one segment at a time a delivery address, read on arrival the next row, in the entry the step just loaded waiting for the address a cache miss on the T-vector a delivery chain a segment, from a flagged start row to the next start the dispatcher one core's instruction stream, interleaving all the lanes' steps the paperwork for each step the instructions a step: the flag test, the byte's store, the pointer and buffer bookkeeping phoning ahead the software prefetch of each lane's next entry the road, the board's size the core's limits: outstanding misses (line fill buffers), the reorder window, the caches deliveries a second for the centre bytes of output a second: throughput, not one load's latency several dispatch centres worker threads, one block each

items.title: Threads
items.text:
• The scanner. One thread reads each block's header and Huffman-coded symbols in order. This is the one sequential phase: a block's end is known only once its symbols are read. It finds blocks exactly, not by searching for the block magic, so a magic inside a block's data is never taken for a block. It is roughly a tenth of a decode on well-compressed text, more on poorly compressible data.
  • The workers. Each worker finishes a block: move-to-front, the T-vector, the inverse BWT walk, RLE1 and the CRC.
  • The reader takes the blocks in order. A block's error reaches the reader only once every block before it has been read.
  • Memory is bounded: at most slots blocks are in flight (by default twice the threads), and the buffers are reused from block to block.

With one thread, the same phases run in order on the calling thread.

items.title: The walk
items.text:
The inverse BWT is a chain of dependent loads: each step's row is the previous step's load. A plain walk keeps one load in flight. The default walk (bwt::walk_segments_room, the flagged walk in passes) keeps many, one a lane (Why 32 couriers beat one explains why, and where it stops paying):

  • 512 pseudo-random rows, the walk's first among them, are segment starts;
  • each start is flagged in its own T-vector entry, which ends the segment before it;
  • 32 lanes walk segments in lockstep, each taking the next segment when its own ends, and each lane's next entry is prefetched as soon as its row is known;
  • the lanes step in passes of room rounds, room the fewest bytes any lane's buffer has spare, each byte written at its lane's base plus the pass's offset, so a step has no pointer store or buffer-end test (after libsais's chain decode, #37);
  • the segments are joined in order.

It equals the plain walk on every list, lists of several cycles included: the join follows the segments' links until the block's length is reached. The flags are cleared before the walk returns. Blocks under 64 Ki are walked plainly. The kernel is behind bwt::InverseBwt (Segmented, the default; Plain), so a walk can be swapped and timed as part of the whole decoder.

items.title: Kernels
items.text: Kernels::detect() chooses at run time: AVX2 (with BMI1) for move-to-front and RLE1, and PCLMULQDQ for the CRC. Each has a scalar twin, used on any other CPU and on aarch64 (Kernels::scalar()). The walk's gain is scalar code, memory-level parallelism, so it holds on any CPU.

items.title: Prior work
items.text:
• The format and its checks are libbzip2's (Julian Seward, bzip2 1.0.8, decompress.c). mibz2 follows its decoding rules and makes each of its checks, in its terms. Its Huffman decode tables are built as BZ2_hbCreateDecodeTables builds them, so a stream libbzip2 refuses is refused here too. It is a separate implementation in Rust, not a port of libbzip2's code. The tests use libbzip2 itself (the bzip2 crate's bundled 1.0.8) as the oracle.
  • Interleaving several traversals of one BWT inversion on one thread, so that out-of-order execution keeps their loads in flight, is Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi's idea: "Slashing the Time for BWT Inversion", DCC 2012, pp. 99–108.
    • They also use a super-alphabet (an LF² table: two characters a dependent lookup) and "Precopy" for repetitive data. Neither is used here: both were built in mibz2 and lost (why).
    • What is particular here is only how the traversals are found in an existing bzip2 file, which carries no metadata for them: the random starts, the flagged starts that end each segment, and the joining in order.
  • libsais (Ilya Grebnov), 2.12's cyclic inverse BWT, "as used by bzip2": its RUN_LANES store, 16 equal last-column bytes linked at once, is in mibz2's T-vector build. Its chain decode's shared-offset passes are mibz2's walk since 0.1.5 (#37).
  • Block-parallel decoding is lbzip2's (Mikołaj Izdebski) and pbzip2's approach.
  • pbz2 (Soof Golan) arrived independently at a segmented, multi-chain walk too; the bake-off that found it is in the journals.

items.title: Python
items.text:
mibz2 needs Python 3.10 or later. It has no Python dependencies.

pip install mibz2

or with uv:

uv add mibz2

Wheels are built for Linux (x86-64, aarch64), macOS (x86-64, arm64) and Windows (x64). Each uses the stable ABI (abi3), so one wheel covers every Python version from 3.10.

items.title: Rust
items.text:
cargo add mibz2

The library depends on std only. Its minimum supported Rust version is 1.80. The python feature builds the Python extension module, and is only for maturin.

items.title: Python
items.text:
Write a .bz2 file with the standard library's bz2, to have one to read:

import bz2

with bz2.open("sample.bz2", "wb") as f:
    for i in range(10_000):
        f.write(f"line {i}\n".encode())

A whole file in memory, decoded on every CPU this process may use, or on one thread:

>>> import mibz2
>>> compressed = open("sample.bz2", "rb").read()
>>> data = mibz2.decompress(compressed)
>>> data == bz2.decompress(compressed)
True
>>> mibz2.decompress(compressed, threads=1) == data
True

A file read as it is decoded: open takes a path or a binary file object, and returns a buffered binary file. Its raw.verified turns true once a read has reached the end with every block's and stream's CRC matched:

>>> with mibz2.open("sample.bz2") as f:
...     first = f.readline()
...     before = f.raw.verified
...     rest = f.read()
...     after = f.raw.verified
>>> first, before, after
(b'line 0\n', False, True)

A bad input raises mibz2.DecodeError, a ValueError, from decompress or from the read at which it is found. The message says which block and bit decoding failed at:

>>> damaged = bytearray(compressed)
>>> damaged[len(damaged) // 2] ^= 0x10
>>> try:
...     mibz2.decompress(bytes(damaged))
... except mibz2.DecodeError as e:
...     print(type(e).__name__, isinstance(e, ValueError))
DecodeError True

items.title: Rust
items.text:
use std::io::Read;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // a whole .bz2 in memory (its streams one after another): on this thread, or on 4
    let data = std::fs::read("file.bz2")?;
    let text = mibz2::decode(&data)?;
    let same = mibz2::decode_parallel(&data, 4)?;
    assert_eq!(text, same);

    // any Read, as a Read: on this thread, or block-parallel on 4 worker threads
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    mibz2::BzReader::parallel(std::fs::File::open("file.bz2")?, 4).read_to_end(&mut out)?;
    Ok(())
}

A bad stream is an mibz2::Error (its kind, block and bit), or from a BzReader an io::Error of kind InvalidData wrapping it. The Rust reference lists the rest: the push decoder, the block scanner and the decoding of a range of blocks.

items.text: path contents src/ the crate: the bit reader, block parsing, MTF, the inverse BWT, RLE1, the CRC, streams, the parallel decoder, BzReader, and python.rs (the extension module, feature python) tests/ the Rust tests against libbzip2 (decode.rs, corpus.rs), their corpora in tests/common/ examples/ ab (the A/B harness), bzcat, fuzz (a mutation fuzz loop), windows (real dump windows checked) benches/ cargo bench bench/ the CI benchmark's scripts and its pinned Wikidata windows python/mibz2/ the Python package, and _mibz2.pyi, the stub of the compiled module python/tests/ the Python tests docs/site/ this site; docs/journal/ the development journals

items.title: Building and testing
items.text:
The tools: a Rust toolchain, uv, just, and for the lints taplo, whitespace-format and cargo-machete.

just py         # maturin develop, then pytest
just test-ci    # cargo test and the doc tests
just clippy     # clippy on every target and feature, warnings as errors
just pc         # formatting and lints (as pre-commit runs them)
cargo test --release                                   # against libbzip2
cargo run --release --example fuzz -- 600 1            # a mutation fuzz loop, libbzip2 the oracle
cargo run --release --example bzcat -- 4 < f.bz2 > f   # the parallel decoder as a command

On aarch64: rustup target add aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu, apt install qemu-user gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu, then cargo test --release --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu --config .cargo/aarch64-qemu.toml.

The segmented walks' unsafe code also runs under Miri, on blocks small enough to interpret: cargo +nightly miri test --lib -- miri_ (about a minute; CI runs it on changes to src/bwt.rs). Those tests assert they reached the transitions the walks' handoffs guard (a buffer growing, a pass ending with a buffer full, a lane coming into the tail full, and so on), so a walk change that stops them reaching one fails rather than passing having checked less.

items.title: Benchmarking
items.text:
Performance is measured on CI (.github/workflows/bench.yml, the benchmark): a pull request that touches the decoder gets a comment with its head against its base. Locally, the same harness:

cargo build --release --example ab
target/release/examples/ab gen corpora 4
target/release/examples/ab run runs.jsonl --arms mibz2,pbz2,lbzip2 --threads 1,4 --rounds 5 corpora/*.bz2
target/release/examples/ab summary runs.jsonl

Where the parallel decoder's time goes as its thread count grows (#39) is measured by the occupancy instrument (examples/occupancy.rs, feature trace), run on the pinned Wikidata corpus by one recipe on any machine, as CI's Occupancy workflow does:

just bench-occupancy                             # 1, 2, 4, ... up to the CPUs allowed
just bench-occupancy --threads 1,2,4,8,12,16,20

It needs cargo, python3, git and lbzip2, and writes occupancy-<UTC time>.json: the machine as the process sees it, each thread count's throughput and the cost of tracing, and the decoder's own timeline (workers decoding or idle and why, the scanner, the reader, and per block its CPU time and run-queue wait). It is a diagnostic: the benchmark's paired A/B decides what is faster.

The benchmark has a version of its own (BENCH in bench/report.py), with its history in bench/CHANGELOG.md: - A pull request that changes the benchmark (bench/, examples/ab.rs, examples/phases.rs, .github/workflows/bench.yml) either adds a changelog entry with its new version, or says in its description why no version is needed. - A major version that redefines a family of figures adds itself to that family in MEANING (bench/report.py), so the site's history splits that family there and joins the others across it. - python3 bench/test_report.py checks that BENCH and the newest entry agree, and that the history joins versions but never runner models, core counts, corpora or a corpus's different contents.

items.title: Commits
items.text: Commit messages follow Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, docs:, ci: ...); the conventional-pre-commit hook checks them. release-plz.toml groups the changelog by these prefixes.

items.title: Documentation
items.text:
The site is built with Zensical from docs/site/ and zensical.toml. The Python API reference is generated by mkdocstrings from the package's docstrings and the compiled module's stub (python/mibz2/_mibz2.pyi).

just docs-serve   # build, serve and rebuild on change
just docs-check   # strict build, site checks, and the pages' examples as tests
  • docs/scripts/check_site.py checks that every page is in the nav, that internal links and anchors resolve, that every page has a description matching its llms.txt entry, and that every public name is in the API reference.
  • docs/conftest.py runs each page's Python examples with pytest (pytest docs/site); a pycon block's output must match.
  • docs/scripts/bench_history.py turns the bench-results branch into the benchmark pages' data (docs/site/assets/bench-history.json) and tables (docs/generated/) before each build. Without a checkout of the branch (--store), it reads origin/bench-results, or writes empty ones.
  • docs/site/assets/data/lane-sweeps.json holds the measured walk timings by lane count that Why 32 couriers beat one draws (assets/javascripts/couriers.js). It is written by hand, from the record: one panel a sweep, each with its own axes, its points (x, y, and optionally lo and hi for an interval) and its source. A new sweep is a new panel; the page draws every panel. Only measured points go in it.

items.title: Publishing
items.text: .github/workflows/site.yml builds the site on every push to master, and after each Benchmark run on master, and publishes it to the gh-pages branch, served at https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/. A pull request from this repository gets a preview under pr-preview/pr-<number>/, linked from a comment on the pull request and removed when it closes. Previews start once the repository's Pages source is set to the gh-pages branch.

items.title: Releasing
items.text: The crate and the Python package are released at one version, from one commit.

items.title: Deploy Release
items.text:
Run the Deploy Release workflow (deploy.yml) with a bump (patch, minor or major). It runs just release, which:

  1. bumps the version in pyproject.toml (uv version --bump) and sets the crate's in Cargo.toml to match;
  2. writes the crate's changelog with release-plz;
  3. commits chore(release): bump 🐍 -> vX.Y.Z and tags py-X.Y.Z;
  4. pushes the commit and the tag, then starts CI on the tag (a tag pushed with the workflow's token starts no workflow by itself).

CI on a py-* tag builds the wheels and the sdist and publishes them to PyPI, and publishes the crate to crates.io with release-plz (which tags mibz2-vX.Y.Z and makes the GitHub release). Both use Trusted Publishing, in the pypi and crates-io environments.

items.title: Out-of-band cases
items.text:
• Tag Release (tag.yml): tags an existing commit py-<version> at the version its pyproject.toml and Cargo.toml already hold (no bump), and starts CI on the tag. Each registry is skipped where it already has the version.
  • Release Notes (release-notes.yml): makes a version's GitHub release (v<version>) at a given commit if it does not exist, or updates its notes, from that version's section of CHANGELOG.md.

items.title: Release notes: the evidence
items.text:
Every version's section of CHANGELOG.md is the GitHub release's notes, so it carries the release's evidence. release-plz writes a one-line entry per commit (and only for commits that touch the crate's files). After the release, rewrite the section by hand:

  1. Dispatch the tag-to-tag bench. Run Benchmark (bench.yml) from the Actions tab with Use workflow from the new tag and base the previous tag:

    gh workflow run bench.yml --ref vX.Y.Z -f base=vX.Y.W

    It is a paired A/B like a pull request's (the base's own harness binary as the arm mibz2@base/ab, the order alternating round to round), on one runner. Its figures are the run's summary and its artifact (bench-pr-<sha>: result.json, comment.md, runs.jsonl, stages.jsonl); nothing is recorded. The base needs examples/ab.rs, and the stage table needs examples/phases.rs (v0.1.2 on); v0.1.3 and v0.1.4 have run as bases this way. The comment's "the merge base with master" means the base given.

  2. Write the entry to the template below, from that run alone, in a pull request. Never add up or chain the pull requests' figures: they were measured against other bases, often on other runner CPUs. A section holds no line starting ## [ (Release Notes ends the section there), so its headings are ### and below.

  3. Re-run Release Notes (release-notes.yml) once the pull request is merged, with the version and its release commit, so the GitHub release takes the section from master.

items.title: The template
items.text:
## [X.Y.Z](https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/compare/vX.Y.W...vX.Y.Z) - YYYY-MM-DD

One or two sentences: what changed for a user, and the release's own Wikidata figure at
1 thread and at the runner's cores, from the tag-to-tag run.

### Measured: vX.Y.Z against vX.Y.W

| corpus | threads | wall, vX.Y.W → vX.Y.Z (median) | wall change (95% interval) | peak RSS | same bytes |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|

Peak RSS, same bytes, and the stage table's rows for any stage a change moved (with the
total), as bullets.

<details><summary>Reproducing this run</summary>

The rerun command and the artifact's name; both tags' full SHAs; the runner's CPU, cores,
clock, kernel and image; rustc; the bench version, rounds and threads; the corpora's bytes
and full SHA-256s (`result.json`'s `corpora`).

</details>

### <!-- 3 -->Performance (one heading per group: Features, Bug Fixes, ...)

- **The change, in a few words** ([#N](https://github.com/lmmx/mibz2/pull/N))
  - *Mechanism:* one or two sentences.
  - *Measured, in its pull request:* its own paired figures, with the runner CPU.
  - *Trade-offs:* what got slower or bigger, and why it was kept.
  - *Evidence:* the bench comment, its runs, the journal entry.

### Downstream: wikidata-pq (if it exists; marked measured or modelled)
  • Decoder figures and downstream figures stay apart. wikidata-pq's figures go under their own heading, each marked measured (a run, linked) or modelled (what the model assumes).
  • Measurement-only and docs-only changes get one line each: what they add, and that the decoder's figures did not change.
  • Rejected experiments go in the journal (docs/journal/), not the changelog.

items.title: mibz2 (Rust)
items.text:
The crate's API documentation is on docs.rs.

API what decode, decode_parallel(data, threads) a whole .bz2 in memory BzReader::new(r), BzReader::parallel(r, threads), parallel_with(r, threads, slots, kernels) a Read adaptor; a bad stream is an io::Error (InvalidData) wrapping mibz2::Error StreamDecoder::new(threads, slots, kernels) the push form: write compressed chunks from one thread, read decoded bytes from another, close, cancel; at most slots blocks in flight scan(data) → BlockSpan { index, start_bit, end_bit, crc, stream, level } block boundaries, without decoding decode_blocks(data, start_bit, end_bit, level, kernels, out) → Range a range of whole blocks, each CRC checked Error { kind: ErrorKind, block, bit } what is wrong with the input, and where Kernels::detect(), Kernels::scalar() the SIMD kernels, or the portable ones bwt::InverseBwt (Segmented, the default; Plain), decode_with::<I>, StreamDecoder::with_inverse::<I> the inverse-BWT kernel, swappable and timeable as part of the whole decoder 
// the block boundaries (each block's header and Huffman symbols read, nothing decoded),
// then any range of whole blocks decoded on its own, on any thread
let data = std::fs::read("file.bz2")?;
for span in mibz2::scan(&data) {
    let span = span?;
    let mut part = Vec::new();
    let range = mibz2::decode_blocks(&data, span.start_bit, span.end_bit, span.level,
                                      mibz2::Kernels::detect(), &mut part)?;
    // range.blocks: each block's (start bit, end bit, CRC); mibz2::combine(...) gives a
    // stream's combined CRC from its blocks'
}

items.title: mibz2
items.text:
mibz2: a fast bzip2 decoder, block-parallel and multi-chain within each block.

  • decompress: a whole .bz2 in memory, decoded.
  • open: a .bz2 file (a path or a binary file object) read as a buffered binary file, decoded as it is read.

Every block's CRC is checked before any of that block's bytes are returned, and each stream's combined CRC is checked at the stream's end. Bytes read from a stream before its end come from blocks whose own CRCs matched, but the stream as a whole is verified only when a read reaches its end: until then, treat what has been read as provisional (see BZ2Reader.verified).

items.title: DecodeError
items.text:
Bases: ValueError

The input is not valid bzip2 data.

items.title: decompress
items.text:
decompress(data: bytes | bytearray, threads: int | None = None) -> bytes

Decode a whole .bz2 (its streams one after another), every CRC checked.

It runs on every CPU this process may use, or on threads.

Raises:

Type Description DecodeError

When the input is not valid bzip2 data.

items.title: BZ2Reader
items.text:
BZ2Reader(source: Source, threads: int | None = None)

Bases: RawIOBase

A .bz2 file's decoded bytes, read in order (an unbuffered binary file).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default source Source

A path, or a binary file object open for reading (its read is called).

required threads int | None

Decoding threads: 1 decodes on the reading thread; more decode that many blocks at once on worker threads. None (the default) uses every CPU this process may use.

None

Raises:

Type Description DecodeError

From a read, when the input is not valid bzip2 data: a block whose CRC does not match (none of its bytes are returned), a stream whose combined CRC does not match (raised by the read that reaches the stream's end), or a malformed or truncated stream. The error says which block and bit it was found at, which is where decoding failed and need not be where the input was damaged.

items.title: readable
items.text:
readable() -> bool

True: a reader is readable.

items.title: readinto
items.text:
readinto(b) -> int

Read up to len(b) decoded bytes into b; 0 at the end (when verified).

items.title: verified property
items.text:
verified: bool

True once a read has reached the end and every block's and stream's CRC matched.

Until then, the bytes read so far have each passed their block's CRC, but the stream's combined CRC has not yet been checked.

items.title: close
items.text:
close() -> None

Stop decoding (its worker threads stop) and close the reader.

items.title: open
items.text:
open(
    source: Source, threads: int | None = None, buffer_size: int = 1 << 20
) -> BufferedReader[BZ2Reader]

Open a .bz2 file for reading, decoded as it is read.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default source Source

A path, or a binary file object open for reading.

required threads int | None

Decoding threads, as for BZ2Reader.

None buffer_size int

The buffered reader's buffer, in bytes.

1 << 20

Returns:

Type Description BufferedReader

A buffered binary file over a BZ2Reader (its raw), whose raw.verified says whether the whole input has been read and verified.

Examples:

>>> import bz2, mibz2, tempfile, os
>>> path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "a.bz2")
>>> with bz2.open(path, "wb") as f:
...     _ = f.write(b"line one\nline two\n")
>>> with mibz2.open(path) as f:
...     lines = f.readlines()
...     verified = f.raw.verified
>>> lines, verified
([b'line one\n', b'line two\n'], True)
